what: The heuristic precomputes CVRP-specific static information during construction by scanning propositional fact names for customers and the depot, storing the grounded fact objects needed to test visited and current-location predicates. It reconstructs direct and via-depot distance matrices from grounded operator names and their metric costs. It also attempts to read demand, capacity, max-vehicles, load, and vehicles numeric variables by name patterns, with graceful fallbacks if they are not directly exposed. In each state, the heuristic reads the visited set and current location from propositional facts and reads current load and vehicle count from numeric variables. It then greedily builds the remaining routes: from the current node it repeatedly chooses the cheapest feasible unvisited customer among direct continuation visits and new-route visit-via-depot transitions, respecting capacity and vehicle limits whenever those values are available. After all customers are visited, it adds the return-to-depot cost if the route is not already at the depot. The returned value is the total estimated remaining routing cost.
why: CVRP solution cost is determined primarily by the order of remaining customer visits and the points where new vehicle routes are started. A greedy nearest-feasible-insertion construction is a natural, efficiently computable estimate of this remaining cost and directly uses the actual action costs from the grounded task rather than fragile derived numeric-variable names. It models the current route state, including current load and used vehicles, which makes it sensitive to capacity and vehicle-count constraints. The precomputed distance and fact structures keep each heuristic evaluation cheap enough for search, while fallbacks ensure the heuristic still runs even when the planner compiles numeric fluents into less transparent expressions.
